title: Daimyo Oak: Ancient Daimyo Oaks You Can Visit
meta_description: Its leaves wrap the rice cakes eaten at Japan's Children's Day and hang on brown through winter. Three daimyo oaks mapped, one growing upside down.
intro: Kashiwa, the daimyo oak, is a slow tree of poor ground and cold slopes that rarely puts on real bulk, which makes every specimen here worth the detour on size alone. Its broad leaves are the reason most people in Japan know the species without knowing they do: they wrap the rice cakes eaten at Children's Day, chosen because the old leaves cling on through winter and let go only when new buds push them off, read as a family line that never breaks. Sapporo's stands on the path to Hokkaido Shrine's worship hall, probably the largest of several big kashiwa on those grounds. Hiroshima's carries the same three-century age band as the giant cedar it grows beside. The oldest and strangest is Shogen-in's Sakasa Gashiwa in Shiwa, its trunk splitting into four limbs at ground level that run outward before turning up, so the branches read as roots that changed their minds; the only daimyo oak under national protection in Japan.
